questions.stem: The volume of liquid delivered from a burette in a titration is best recorded as
questions.explanation: Burette readings are recorded to two decimal places (the second place being 0 or 5).

questions.stem: Which apparatus measures a fixed volume of solution most accurately?
questions.explanation: A pipette delivers a single fixed volume (e.g. 25.0 cm^3) with high accuracy.

questions.stem: A suggested explanation of an observation that can be tested by experiment is called a
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation that is then tested by experiments.

questions.stem: In a scientific investigation, the factor deliberately changed by the experimenter is the
questions.explanation: The independent variable is varied; the dependent variable is measured; others are kept constant.

questions.stem: A student weighed an empty crucible as 18.42 g and the crucible with a sample as 21.07 g. The mass of the sample is
The particle found in the nucleus of an atom that carries no charge is the
questions.explanation: Neutrons are neutral; protons are positive and electrons (outside the nucleus) are negative.

questions.stem: The discovery of the electron is credited to
questions.explanation: Thomson identified the electron from cathode-ray experiments; Chadwick discovered the neutron.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: An atom of an element has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 atoms differ in their
questions.explanation: Both have 6 protons and 6 electrons; carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, carbon-12 has 6.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: Boron consists of 20% of boron-10 and 80% of boron-11. Its relative atomic mass is

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: Chlorine has isotopes of mass numbers 35 and 37 and relative atomic mass 35.5. The percentage of chlorine-37 is
questions.explanation: 35x + 37(100 - x) = 3550 gives 2x = 150, x = 75% chlorine-35, so chlorine-37 is 25%.

questions.topic: Particulate nature of matter: physical and chemical changes
questions.stem: A trader notices several changes in her shop. Which one involves the formation of a new substance?
questions.explanation: Souring of palm wine is fermentation to ethanoic acid, a chemical change; the others are physical changes.

questions.topic: Particulate nature of matter: physical and chemical changes
questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a physical change?
options: The mass of the substance changes
It is accompanied by a large energy change
questions.explanation: Physical changes form no new substance and are usually easily reversible.

questions.stem: Which sub-level is filled immediately after 3p according to the Aufbau principle?
questions.explanation: The 4s sub-level has lower energy than 3d and is filled first (as in K and Ca).

questions.stem: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a p sub-level is
questions.explanation: A p sub-level has three orbitals, each holding two electrons.

questions.stem: Which principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers?
questions.explanation: Pauli's exclusion principle limits each orbital to two electrons of opposite spin.

questions.stem: The number of unpaired electrons in a nitrogen atom (1s2 2s2 2p3) in its ground state is
questions.explanation: By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins.

questions.stem: Garri mixed with sand can best be separated by
questions.explanation: Garri grains and sand grains differ in size, so a sieve of suitable mesh separates them.

questions.stem: A village near the coast wants drinking water from sea water using sunlight to evaporate the water and a cool cover to collect the droplets. The process is essentially
questions.explanation: Evaporation followed by condensation of the vapour is distillation (a solar still).

questions.stem: A mixture of ammonium chloride and sodium chloride can be separated by
questions.explanation: Ammonium chloride sublimes on heating, leaving sodium chloride behind.

questions.stem: A mechanic accidentally pours engine oil into a bucket of water. The oil forms a separate top layer. The best laboratory method to recover the oil is
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids form layers that can be run off separately from a separating funnel.

questions.stem: In a paper chromatogram, a dye moved 4.5 cm while the solvent front moved 12.0 cm. The Rf value of the dye is
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by dye/distance moved by solvent = 4.5/12.0 = 0.375.

questions.stem: Fractional distillation is used to separate liquids that
options: are immiscible and form two separate layers
are miscible and have different boiling points
questions.explanation: Miscible liquids with different boiling points are separated by fractional distillation, as in crude oil refining.

questions.stem: Element X has atomic number 16. In the periodic table X is found in
questions.explanation: Configuration 2, 8, 6: three shells (Period 3) and six valence electrons (Group 6/16) - sulphur.

questions.topic: Categories of elements in the periodic table
questions.stem: Germanium is classified as a metalloid because it
options: is a typical alkali metal in Group 1 of the table
has properties of both metals and non-metals
is a liquid at room temperature
has no electrons in its outer shell
questions.explanation: Metalloids such as Ge, Si and As show intermediate properties, e.g. semiconduction.

questions.topic: Categories of elements in the periodic table
questions.stem: The elements of Group 1 are called alkali metals because they
options: form hydroxides that are soluble and strongly basic
react only with alkalis and never with acids or water
questions.explanation: Group 1 metals react with water to give soluble, strongly alkaline hydroxides.

questions.stem: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally
questions.explanation: Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, pulling them closer.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of the Group 1 elements decrease from lithium to caesium mainly because
options: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded
questions.explanation: Down the group the atomic radius and shielding increase, so the outer electron is held less firmly.

questions.stem: Electronegativity increases
options: across a period and decreases down a group
both across a period and down a group
down a group and decreases across a period
questions.explanation: Smaller atoms with greater nuclear charge attract bonding electrons more strongly.

questions.topic: Reactions of acids with metals, oxides and trioxocarbonates (IV)
questions.stem: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to marble chips, the gas evolved is
questions.explanation: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

questions.topic: Reactions of acids with metals, oxides and trioxocarbonates (IV)
questions.stem: Zinc reacts with dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid to produce
questions.explanation: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2.

questions.stem: Which halogen is the strongest oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: Oxidising power decreases down Group 7; fluorine, the smallest atom, gains electrons most readily.

questions.stem: When chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium bromide, the solution turns orange-brown because
options: chlorine displaces bromine from the bromide
bromine displaces chlorine from the chloride
questions.explanation: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2; chlorine is a stronger oxidant than bromine.

questions.topic: Elements of the first transition series
questions.stem: Iron forms both FeCl2 and FeCl3. This illustrates that transition metals
questions.explanation: Iron shows +2 and +3 oxidation states, a typical transition-metal property.

questions.topic: Elements of the first transition series
questions.stem: The electron configuration of the Fe^3+ ion (Fe, Z = 26) is
questions.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d6 4s2; the 4s electrons are lost first, then one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d5.

questions.stem: A sodium atom (2, 8, 1) readily loses one electron. This makes it
options: gain a proton and become a different element
attain the stable configuration of neon
questions.explanation: Na+ has the configuration 2, 8, the same as neon.

questions.stem: The bond formed between magnesium and oxygen in magnesium oxide is
questions.explanation: Magnesium transfers two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg^2+ and O^2- ions.

questions.stem: Solid potassium chloride does not conduct electricity, but its aqueous solution does. This is because in solution
options: the ions are free to move
the water conducts on its own
questions.explanation: In the solid the ions are held in a lattice; dissolving frees them to carry charge.

questions.stem: The number of shared pairs of electrons in a molecule of nitrogen, N2, is
questions.explanation: N2 has a triple bond: three shared pairs.

questions.stem: The hydroxonium ion, H3O+, contains a coordinate bond formed when
options: a lone pair on oxygen is donated to a hydrogen ion
two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons
hydrogen donates a lone pair to oxygen
oxygen transfers an electron to hydrogen
questions.explanation: Water donates one of its oxygen lone pairs to H+, giving H3O+.

questions.stem: The ammonia molecule, NH3, with three bonding pairs and one lone pair, has a shape described as
questions.explanation: The lone pair occupies one tetrahedral position, so the atoms form a trigonal pyramid.

questions.stem: The H-O-H bond angle in water (about 104.5 degrees) is smaller than the tetrahedral angle because
options: lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen exert greater repulsion, squeezing the bonding pairs closer.

questions.stem: Copper wire can be drawn out into thin cables without breaking because in metallic bonding
options: the atoms are joined by fixed covalent bonds
the ions repel strongly when moved
layers of ions can slide while the electron sea holds them together
questions.explanation: Non-directional metallic bonding allows layers to move without breaking the structure (ductility).

questions.stem: Water has an unusually high boiling point for its molar mass because of
options: the weakness of the covalent O-H bonds inside it
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between H2O molecules require extra energy to overcome.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances has van der Waals forces as the only attraction between its molecules?
questions.explanation: I2 is non-polar; the others form hydrogen bonds between molecules.

questions.stem: Calcium phosphate, used in fertilisers, contains Ca^2+ and PO4^3- ions. Its formula is
questions.explanation: Three Ca^2+ (+6) balance two PO4^3- (-6).

questions.stem: In the balanced equation aFe + bCl2 -> cFeCl3, the values of a, b and c are
questions.explanation: 2Fe + 3Cl2 -> 2FeCl3 balances iron (2) and chlorine (6).

questions.stem: A bag contains 117 g of table salt, NaCl. The amount of salt in moles is (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
questions.explanation: Molar mass NaCl = 58.5 g mol^-1; n = 117/58.5 = 2.0 mol.

questions.stem: The number of molecules in 3.6 g of water is (H = 1, O = 16, L = 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1)
The volume occupied by 0.25 mol of oxygen at s.t.p. is (molar volume = 22.4 dm^3)
A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
Urea, CO(NH2)2, is a nitrogen fertiliser. Its percentage by mass of nitrogen is (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1)
What mass of calcium oxide is obtained by heating 25 g of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) to constant mass? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; 100 g gives 56 g, so 25 g gives 14 g.

questions.stem: What volume of hydrogen at s.t.p. is produced when 2.4 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid? (Mg = 24, molar volume = 22.4 dm^3)
questions.explanation: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2; 0.10 mol Mg gives 0.10 mol H2 = 2.24 dm^3.

questions.stem: In the reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, 6.0 g of hydrogen reacts with excess nitrogen. The mass of ammonia formed is (N = 14, H = 1)
questions.explanation: 6.0 g H2 = 3.0 mol, giving 2.0 mol NH3 = 2.0 x 17 = 34 g.

questions.stem: A solution contains 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide in 500 cm^3. Its concentration is (NaOH = 40 g mol^-1)
The mass concentration of a 0.050 mol dm^-3 solution of anhydrous sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3, is (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass 106 g mol^-1; 0.050 x 106 = 5.3 g dm^-3.

questions.stem: A standard solution is one whose
options: solute is a primary standard only
questions.explanation: A standard solution has an accurately known concentration.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide is not suitable as a primary standard because it
options: absorbs moisture and carbon(IV) oxide from the air
has a very high molar mass
questions.explanation: NaOH is deliquescent and absorbs CO2, so its mass cannot be weighed accurately.

questions.stem: A technician dilutes 25.0 cm^3 of 4.0 mol dm^-3 tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid to 500 cm^3 with distilled water. The concentration of the diluted acid is
To what final volume must 40 cm^3 of 1.5 mol dm^-3 potassium hydroxide be diluted to give a 0.25 mol dm^-3 solution?
According to the kinetic theory, the particles of a substance have the highest average kinetic energy in the
questions.explanation: At a higher temperature in the gaseous state, particles move fastest and have the most kinetic energy.

questions.stem: The direct change of a solid to vapour without melting is called
questions.explanation: Iodine and naphthalene sublime on warming.

questions.stem: During the melting of a pure solid, the temperature remains constant because the heat absorbed is used to
options: increase the kinetic energy of the particles
overcome the forces holding the particles in fixed positions
break covalent bonds within the molecules
questions.explanation: The latent heat increases potential energy by loosening the lattice, not the average kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Under the same conditions, which gas diffuses fastest? (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Cl = 35.5)
questions.explanation: Rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass; methane (16) is the lightest listed.

questions.stem: Under the same conditions, the ratio of the rate of diffusion of hydrogen to that of oxygen is (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Rate(H2)/Rate(O2) = sqrt(32/2) = sqrt(16) = 4.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 200 cm^3 at 27 degrees C and 1.0 atm. At 1.0 atm and 127 degrees C, its volume is
A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 380 cm^3 at 27 degrees C and 750 mmHg. Its volume at s.t.p. (273 K, 760 mmHg) is
Which of the following conditions makes a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
options: Very high pressure at any temperature
questions.explanation: At high temperature and low pressure, intermolecular forces and molecular volume become negligible.

questions.stem: A vapour differs from a gas in that a vapour
options: can be liquefied by pressure alone at that temperature
questions.explanation: A vapour is below its critical temperature and so can be liquefied by compression alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following solids has a giant ionic lattice?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride consists of Na+ and Cl- ions in a giant lattice; iodine, ice and sulphur are molecular, diamond is giant covalent.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity whereas diamond does not because in graphite
options: each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds
the layers are held by strong covalent bonds
each carbon atom has one delocalised electron
questions.explanation: Each carbon in graphite uses three electrons in bonding, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.

questions.stem: Graphite is used as a lubricant because
options: its layers can slide over one another
questions.explanation: Weak forces between the layers allow them to slide easily.

questions.stem: Silicon(IV) oxide has a very high melting point because it
options: has a giant covalent structure with strong bonds throughout
questions.explanation: Melting requires breaking many strong Si-O covalent bonds in the giant network.

questions.stem: A cold pack for sports injuries becomes cold when the salt inside dissolves. The dissolving process is
questions.explanation: Heat is absorbed from the surroundings, so the process is endothermic (Delta H positive).

questions.stem: For an endothermic reaction, the enthalpy change Delta H is
options: always greater than the activation energy
questions.explanation: Products have more enthalpy than reactants, so Delta H > 0.

questions.stem: When ammonium chloride dissolves in water, the beaker feels cold. This shows that the dissolution is
questions.explanation: Heat is absorbed from the water and the surroundings, so the temperature falls.

questions.stem: When 50 cm^3 of 1.0 mol dm^-3 HCl is mixed with 50 cm^3 of 1.0 mol dm^-3 NaOH, the temperature rises by 6.8 K. Taking the specific heat capacity of the solution as 4.2 J g^-1 K^-1 and its density as 1.0 g cm^-3, the enthalpy of neutralisation is
questions.explanation: Heat = 100 x 4.2 x 6.8 = 2856 J for 0.050 mol water: 2856/0.050 = 57 120 J mol^-1, so Delta H = -57.1 kJ mol^-1.

questions.stem: Given C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g), Delta H = -394 kJ mol^-1, the heat released when 3.0 g of carbon burns completely is (C = 12)
A spontaneous reaction at constant temperature and pressure is one for which the change in Gibbs free energy, Delta G, is
questions.explanation: Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S; a negative Delta G indicates a feasible (spontaneous) change.

questions.stem: The energy barrier that reactant particles must overcome before they react is the
questions.explanation: Only collisions with at least the activation energy lead to reaction.

questions.stem: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance which
options: produces hydrogen ions as the only positive ions in water
produces hydroxide ions as the only negative ions in water
questions.explanation: Arrhenius acids ionise in water to give H+ (H3O+) as the only cations.

questions.stem: In the reaction NH3 + H2O <=> NH4+ + OH-, water acts as a
questions.explanation: Water donates a proton to ammonia, so it is acting as a Bronsted-Lowry acid.

questions.stem: Tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is described as dibasic because one molecule
options: reacts with two bases at once
produces two hydrogen ions on complete ionisation
questions.explanation: Basicity is the number of replaceable hydrogen ions per molecule: H2SO4 -> 2H+ + SO4^2-.

questions.stem: A sample of rainwater has a hydrogen ion concentration of 1.0 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3. Its pH is
questions.explanation: pH = -log(1.0 x 10^-5) = 5 (acid rain).

questions.stem: The pH of a 0.01 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution at 25 degrees C is
A salt formed when only part of the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal is called
questions.explanation: E.g. NaHSO4 and NaHCO3 are acid salts.

questions.stem: Which of the following salts is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: PbSO4 is insoluble; all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts and all trioxonitrates(V) are soluble.

questions.stem: Which method is most suitable for preparing a pure, dry sample of insoluble silver chloride?
questions.explanation: Mixing solutions of AgNO3 and NaCl precipitates AgCl, which is filtered, washed and dried.

questions.stem: An aqueous solution of sodium ethanoate is
questions.explanation: Ethanoate ions (from a weak acid) hydrolyse: CH3COO- + H2O <=> CH3COOH + OH-, giving an alkaline solution.

questions.stem: A solution of iron(III) chloride turns blue litmus red. This is because
options: iron(III) chloride is a covalent gas
iron(III) chloride is a strong base
the Fe^3+ ions hydrolyse to release hydrogen ions
questions.explanation: Hydrated Fe^3+ ions hydrolyse: Fe^3+ + 3H2O <=> Fe(OH)3 + 3H+, making the solution acidic.

questions.stem: Washing soda crystals, Na2CO3.10H2O, left in open air lose some water of crystallisation. This property is called
questions.explanation: Efflorescent substances give off water of crystallisation to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: For the titration of aqueous ammonia with hydrochloric acid, the most suitable indicator is
questions.explanation: A strong acid/weak base titration has an acidic end-point (pH about 5), matching methyl orange.

questions.stem: Methyl orange in an alkaline solution is
questions.explanation: Methyl orange is red in acid, yellow in alkali, and orange at the end-point.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.10 mol dm^-3 NaOH requires 20.0 cm^3 of HCl for neutralisation. The concentration of the acid is
questions.explanation: Moles NaOH = 0.0025 = moles HCl; C = 0.0025/0.020 = 0.125 mol dm^-3.

questions.stem: 20.0 cm^3 of 0.050 mol dm^-3 H2SO4 exactly neutralises 25.0 cm^3 of KOH solution. The concentration of the KOH is
questions.explanation: H2SO4 + 2KOH -> K2SO4 + 2H2O. Moles acid = 0.0010; KOH = 0.0020 mol in 0.025 dm^3 = 0.080 mol dm^-3.

questions.stem: A solution that can dissolve no more solute at a given temperature is
questions.explanation: A saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute at that temperature.

questions.stem: The solubility of a salt at 30 degrees C is 40 g per 100 g of water. The mass of salt that dissolves in 250 g of water at that temperature is
questions.explanation: 40 g per 100 g water, so 250 g water dissolves 100 g.

questions.stem: A saturated solution of potassium trioxonitrate(V) contains 22.0 g of salt in 50.0 g of water at 20 degrees C. Its solubility in mol dm^-3, assuming 50.0 g of water gives 50.0 cm^3 of solution, is (K = 39, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass KNO3 = 101; n = 22.0/101 = 0.218 mol in 0.050 dm^3 = 4.36 mol dm^-3.

questions.stem: The solubility of most gases in water decreases when
questions.explanation: Gases are less soluble in hot water, which is why fish suffer in warm, polluted rivers.

questions.stem: Crystals of a salt can be obtained from a hot saturated solution by
options: heating it further at constant volume
questions.explanation: Solubility falls on cooling, so excess solute crystallises out.

questions.stem: A salt has a solubility of 80 g per 100 g of water at 60 degrees C and 30 g per 100 g of water at 20 degrees C. The mass of crystals deposited when 90 g of solution saturated at 60 degrees C is cooled to 20 degrees C is
questions.explanation: 90 g of solution contains 40 g salt and 50 g water. At 20 degrees C, 50 g water holds 15 g, so 40 - 15 = 25 g crystallise.

questions.stem: Yam slices cook faster than whole yam tubers of the same mass because the slices
options: contain a natural catalyst for cooking
questions.explanation: Increasing the surface area increases the rate of heat transfer and reaction.

questions.stem: When a little manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution, oxygen is evolved rapidly and the mass of the oxide is unchanged at the end. The manganese(IV) oxide acts as
questions.explanation: It speeds up the decomposition and is recovered unchanged in mass.

questions.stem: According to collision theory, which of the following collisions is most likely to lead to a reaction?
options: A collision with a wall of the container
A gentle collision at low speed
One with enough energy and the correct orientation
questions.explanation: Effective collisions need energy at least equal to the activation energy and a suitable orientation.

questions.stem: In a graph of volume of gas evolved against time for a reaction, the curve becomes horizontal when
options: the rate is at its maximum
one of the reactants is used up
questions.explanation: No more gas is produced once a limiting reactant is exhausted.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess acid; 12 cm^3 of hydrogen is collected after 10 s, 20 cm^3 after 20 s and 24 cm^3 after 30 s. The average rate in the second 10 s interval is
questions.explanation: (20 - 12)/(20 - 10) = 0.80 cm^3 s^-1; the rate falls as the magnesium is used up.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [H2] = 0.20, [I2] = 0.20 and [HI] = 1.6 mol dm^-3. The equilibrium constant Kc is
For the equilibrium CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g), Delta H negative, the yield of methanol is increased by
questions.explanation: Three gas molecules form one; high pressure favours the side with fewer molecules.

questions.stem: In the equilibrium 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), Delta H negative, raising the temperature will
options: increase the rate but leave Kc unchanged
increase the yield of SO3 and raise Kc
leave the yield and Kc unchanged
decrease the yield of SO3 and lower Kc
questions.explanation: For an exothermic forward reaction, higher temperature shifts equilibrium to the left and reduces Kc.

questions.stem: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium
options: changes the value of the equilibrium constant
does not change the position of equilibrium
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally.

questions.stem: The oxidation number of nitrogen in the trioxonitrate(V) ion, NO3^-, is
questions.explanation: N + 3(-2) = -1 gives N = +5, as shown by the name trioxonitrate(V).

questions.stem: The oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate(VI) ion, Cr2O7^2-, and of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S2O3^2-, are respectively
questions.explanation: 2Cr - 14 = -2 gives Cr = +6; 2S - 6 = -2 gives S = +2.

questions.stem: In the reaction CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, the reducing agent is
questions.explanation: Hydrogen removes oxygen from CuO and is itself oxidised.

questions.stem: Which of the following is commonly used as an oxidising agent in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: Acidified K2Cr2O7 is a strong oxidant (orange to green); the others are reducing agents.

questions.stem: In the half-equation MnO4^- + 8H^+ + ne^- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O, the value of n is
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons; charges balance: -1 + 8 - 5 = +2.

questions.stem: In a simple cell made of a magnesium strip and a copper strip dipped in brine, the negative electrode is
options: copper, because it is less reactive
magnesium, because it is less reactive
magnesium, because it is more electropositive
questions.explanation: The more reactive metal loses electrons (is oxidised) and becomes the negative terminal.

questions.stem: Given E(Zn^2+/Zn) = -0.76 V and E(Cu^2+/Cu) = +0.34 V, the e.m.f. of the Daniell cell is
questions.explanation: E cell = E(cathode) - E(anode) = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of acidified water using platinum electrodes, the gas liberated at the anode is
questions.explanation: OH- ions (from water) are discharged at the anode: 4OH- -> 2H2O + O2 + 4e-.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride with inert electrodes, the product at the anode is
questions.explanation: At high Cl- concentration, chloride ions are preferentially discharged at the anode.

questions.stem: The mass of copper deposited when a current of 2.0 A is passed through aqueous copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) for 32 min 10 s is (Cu = 64, F = 96 500 C mol^-1)
questions.explanation: Q = 2.0 x 1930 = 3860 C = 0.040 F; Cu^2+ needs 2 F per mole, so 0.020 mol = 1.28 g.

questions.stem: How many faradays are needed to deposit 5.4 g of aluminium from molten aluminium oxide? (Al = 27)
Rusting of iron requires the presence of
questions.explanation: Iron rusts only when both oxygen and water are present.

questions.stem: Galvanised iron sheets used for roofing are coated with
questions.explanation: Zinc protects iron sacrificially, corroding in preference to iron even when scratched.

questions.stem: Magnesium blocks attached to the hull of a ship protect the steel from corrosion because magnesium
options: reacts with salt to form a protective coat
is more reactive than iron and is oxidised instead
forms an alloy with the steel
questions.explanation: Sacrificial protection: the more electropositive Mg corrodes, keeping the iron as the cathode.

questions.stem: Hydrocarbons are compounds that contain
questions.explanation: A hydrocarbon consists of carbon and hydrogen atoms only.

questions.stem: Cyclohexane, C6H12, is classified as
questions.explanation: Cyclohexane has a ring of single bonds with no delocalised electrons, so it is alicyclic, not aromatic.

questions.stem: The compound CH3CH2CHO belongs to the homologous series of
questions.explanation: The -CHO group at the end of the chain is the aldehyde (alkanal) group: propanal.

questions.topic: Separation and purification of organic compounds
questions.stem: A crude sample of benzoic acid is purified by dissolving it in hot water, filtering and cooling the filtrate. This process is
questions.explanation: Impurities remain in solution while purer crystals separate on cooling.

questions.stem: The process used to separate crude oil into fractions such as petrol and kerosene is
questions.explanation: Crude oil components are separated according to boiling-point ranges in a fractionating tower.

questions.stem: Cracking of petroleum fractions is carried out to
options: produce smaller, more useful molecules such as petrol and alkenes
increase the boiling points of fractions
join small molecules into large ones
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes.

questions.topic: Determination of formulae and structures of organic compounds
questions.stem: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass and has a relative molecular mass of 56. Its molecular formula is (C = 12, H = 1)
Most organic compounds
options: have low melting points and burn readily
questions.explanation: Organic compounds are mostly covalent, with weak intermolecular forces, and are combustible.

questions.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in diffused sunlight by
questions.explanation: Alkanes undergo free-radical substitution: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl.

questions.stem: The number of structural isomers of C5H12 is
questions.explanation: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

questions.stem: The test for unsaturation in an organic compound is that it
options: gives a white precipitate with silver trioxonitrate(V)
questions.explanation: The C=C double bond adds bromine, removing the orange-brown colour.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) atomic number; (ii) mass number; (iii) isotopy. [3 marks]
(b) Magnesium occurs naturally as three isotopes: magnesium-24 (78.99%), magnesium-25 (10.00%) and magnesium-26 (11.01%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium to two decimal places. [4 marks]
(c) An atom Y has 15 protons and 16 neutrons.
(i) Write its electron configuration in terms of s and p orbitals. [2 marks]
(ii) State its group and period in the periodic table. [2 marks]
(iii) How many unpaired electrons does it have in its ground state? Give a reason. [2 marks]
(d)(i) State two observations from Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment and the conclusion drawn from each. [4 marks]
(ii) State two limitations of Dalton's atomic theory in the light of modern knowledge. [2 marks]
(e)(i) State Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity. [2 marks]
(ii) Write the electron configuration of chromium (Z = 24) and explain why it is unusual. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) Atomic number: the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
1 mark: (ii) Mass number: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
1 mark: (iii) Isotopy: the existence of atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers
2 marks: (b) R.A.M. = (78.99 x 24 + 10.00 x 25 + 11.01 x 26)/100
1 mark: = (1895.76 + 250.00 + 286.26)/100
1 mark: = 24.32
2 marks: (c)(i) 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3
1 mark: (ii) Group 5 (15)
1 mark: Period 3
1 mark: (iii) Three unpaired electrons
1 mark: The three 3p electrons occupy separate p orbitals singly with parallel spins (Hund's rule)
2 marks: (d)(i) Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space
2 marks: A few were deflected through large angles/bounced back, so there is a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
2 marks: (d)(ii) Any two: atoms are divisible into protons, neutrons and electrons; atoms of the same element can have different masses (isotopes); atoms can be changed by nuclear reactions (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e)(i) When electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy, they fill them singly with parallel spins before pairing begins
2 marks: (e)(ii) Cr: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s1
2 marks: Unusual because one 4s electron moves into 3d to give a half-filled 3d sub-level, which is more stable than 3d4 4s2
questions.explanation: R.A.M. of Mg = 24.32. Y is phosphorus (2, 8, 5): Group 5, Period 3, three unpaired 3p electrons. Rutherford: empty space and a dense nucleus. Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 because a half-filled d sub-level is extra stable.

questions.stem:
(a) State the periodic law. [2 marks]
(b) The elements P, Q, R and S have atomic numbers 11, 12, 17 and 19 respectively (letters are not the true symbols).

(ii) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. [2 marks]
(e) Explain why chlorine is more reactive than iodine. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers
1 mark: (b)(i) P: 2, 8, 1
1 mark: Q: 2, 8, 2
1 mark: R: 2, 8, 7
1 mark: S: 2, 8, 8, 1
1 mark: (b)(ii) P and S
1 mark: Both have one electron in the outermost shell (Group 1)
1 mark: (b)(iii) S
2 marks: S has four occupied shells, more than the others, so its outer electron is furthest from the nucleus (more shielding)
2 marks: (b)(iv) QR2 (e.g. MgCl2)
1 mark: Ionic (electrovalent) bonding
1 mark: (c) Nuclear charge increases across the period
1 mark: Electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding hardly changes
1 mark: Outer electrons are held more firmly, so more energy is needed to remove one
3 marks: (d)(i) P floats/darts about on the surface (1); melts into a ball and fizzes as a gas is given off (1); the solution turns pink as an alkali forms (1)
2 marks: (d)(ii) 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 (formulae 1, balancing 1)
3 marks: (e) Chlorine atoms are smaller (1); the incoming electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded (1); so chlorine gains an electron (is reduced) more readily (1)
questions.explanation: P = Na (2,8,1), Q = Mg (2,8,2), R = Cl (2,8,7), S = K (2,8,8,1). P and S are Group 1; S is largest; QR2 is ionic. Ionisation energy rises across a period as nuclear charge rises with little extra shielding. Sodium darts about, fizzes and turns phenolphthalein pink: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. Chlorine is smaller, so it attracts electrons more strongly than iodine.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between an ionic bond and a covalent bond. [4 marks]
(b) Using dot-and-cross descriptions in words, explain the bonding in (i) magnesium chloride; (ii) ammonia. [6 marks]
(c) Predict the shapes of the following molecules and give the approximate bond angle in each: (i) CO2; (ii) BF3; (iii) CH4; (iv) H2O. [8 marks]
(d) State three differences in physical properties between sodium chloride and tetrachloromethane. [3 marks]
(e) Explain why ethanol is completely miscible with water while hexane is not. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Ionic bond: formed by complete transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, giving oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction
2 marks: Covalent bond: formed by sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two (usually non-metal) atoms
3 marks: (b)(i) Mg (2,8,2) transfers one electron to each of two Cl atoms (2,8,7) (1); forming Mg^2+ (2,8) and two Cl^- (2,8,8) ions (1); ions held by electrostatic attraction (1)
3 marks: (b)(ii) N (2,5) shares one electron with each of three H atoms (1); forming three N-H shared pairs (1); one lone pair remains on N, giving N an octet and each H a duplet (1)
2 marks: (c)(i) CO2: linear, 180 degrees
2 marks: (ii) BF3: trigonal planar, 120 degrees
2 marks: (iii) CH4: tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees
2 marks: (iv) H2O: V-shaped (bent), about 104.5 degrees
3 marks: (d) NaCl: high melting point, conducts when molten/in solution, soluble in water; CCl4: low boiling liquid, non-conductor, insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (1 mark per contrasted pair)
2 marks: (e) Ethanol contains an -OH group which forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules
2 marks: Hexane is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so it does not mix (forms a separate layer)
questions.explanation: Ionic = electron transfer; covalent = sharing. MgCl2: Mg^2+ and 2Cl^-; NH3: three shared pairs plus a lone pair on N. Shapes: CO2 linear 180, BF3 trigonal planar 120, CH4 tetrahedral 109.5, H2O bent about 104.5 degrees. Ethanol hydrogen-bonds with water; hexane cannot.

2 marks: (ii) Shifts to the left (less SO3): forward reaction is exothermic, so the endothermic backward reaction is favoured
2 marks: (iii) Shifts to the right: more SO2 and O2 react to replace the SO3 removed

1 mark: = 64 (no units)

questions.explanation: Equilibrium concentrations: [H2] = [I2] = 0.040, [HI] = 0.32 mol dm^-3, Kc = 64. High pressure and low temperature favour SO3; a catalyst only speeds attainment of equilibrium.

2 marks: Thermosetting plastics do not soften on reheating (cross-linked) and cannot be remoulded, e.g. bakelite, melamine
1 mark: (d)(i) Starch: glucose
1 mark: Proteins: amino acids
3 marks: (d)(ii) Crush beans in water, add sodium hydroxide solution then a few drops of dilute copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution (Biuret test) (2); a violet/purple colour shows protein (1)
2 marks: (d)(iii) Boil starch solution with dilute HCl/H2SO4 for some minutes; starch is hydrolysed to glucose
2 marks: Neutralise, add Fehling's (or Benedict's) solution and warm: a brick-red precipitate shows a reducing sugar (glucose)
3 marks: (e) Any three: light in weight; do not corrode/rust; good insulators of heat and electricity; easily moulded into shapes; cheaper; can be coloured (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: Addition polymers (poly(ethene)) form without loss of molecules; condensation polymers (nylon) eliminate water/HCl. Thermoplastics can be remoulded; thermosets cannot. Biuret test (violet) for proteins; acid hydrolysis of starch gives glucose (brick-red with Fehling's).

questions.stem:

(f) Give one test for ammonia gas. [2 marks]
[N = 14, H = 1, S = 32, O = 16; molar volume = 22.4 dm^3]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Heat a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide (slaked lime)
2 marks: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3
1 mark: Tube inclined slightly downwards so condensed water does not run back on the hot glass
1 mark: Dry the gas by passing it through a tower of quicklime (CaO)
1 mark: Collect by upward delivery (downward displacement of air), since ammonia is lighter than air
2 marks: (b) Any two: colourless; pungent smell; less dense than air; very soluble in water; easily liquefied (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c)(i) N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3
3 marks: (c)(ii) Finely divided iron catalyst (1); temperature about 450 degrees C (1); pressure about 200 atm (1)

1 mark: (d) Molar mass (NH4)2SO4 = 132 g mol^-1

3 marks: (e) Excess fertiliser is washed into rivers and lakes (1); causes eutrophication/algal bloom (1); decay of algae uses up dissolved oxygen, killing fish; nitrates in drinking water are harmful to infants (1)
2 marks: (f) Turns damp red litmus paper blue / forms dense white fumes with hydrogen chloride from a glass rod dipped in concentrated HCl
questions.explanation: Ammonia is made by heating NH4Cl with Ca(OH)2, dried with CaO and collected by upward delivery. 34 g NH3 (2.0 mol) needs 1.0 mol N2 = 22.4 dm^3 at s.t.p. % N in (NH4)2SO4 = 21.2%.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between temporary hardness and permanent hardness of water, naming the compound responsible for each. [4 marks]
(b) Explain, with equations, how temporary hardness is removed by (i) boiling; (ii) addition of calcium hydroxide in calculated amount. [6 marks]
(c) Explain, with an equation, how washing soda removes permanent hardness. [3 marks]
(d) State two advantages and two disadvantages of hard water. [4 marks]
(e) Describe the stages involved in the treatment of water for a town supply. [6 marks]
(f) Why is soap wasted in hard water? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Temporary hardness can be removed by boiling
1 mark: Caused by calcium (or magnesium) hydrogentrioxocarbonate(IV), Ca(HCO3)2
1 mark: Permanent hardness cannot be removed by boiling
1 mark: Caused by calcium/magnesium tetraoxosulphate(VI) or chloride
3 marks: (b)(i) On boiling, Ca(HCO3)2 decomposes: Ca(HCO3)2 -> CaCO3 + H2O + CO2; CaCO3 is precipitated (scale)
3 marks: (ii) Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2CaCO3 + 2H2O; insoluble CaCO3 precipitates and is filtered off (Clark's method)
1 mark: (c) Washing soda precipitates calcium and magnesium ions as insoluble trioxocarbonates(IV)
2 marks: CaSO4 + Na2CO3 -> CaCO3 + Na2SO4
2 marks: (d) Advantages (any two): provides calcium for bones and teeth; pleasant taste; does not dissolve lead from pipes; good for brewing
2 marks: Disadvantages (any two): wastes soap; forms scale in kettles and boilers; stains clothes and sinks; blocks hot-water pipes
6 marks: (e) Screening to remove large debris (1); sedimentation in a reservoir (1); coagulation with alum (aluminium tetraoxosulphate(VI)) (1); filtration through sand/gravel beds (1); chlorination to kill germs (1); storage and distribution (pH adjustment with lime) (1)
2 marks: (f) Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ ions react with soap to form insoluble scum, so no lather forms until all the ions have been precipitated
questions.explanation: Temporary hardness (Ca(HCO3)2) is removed by boiling or Clark's method; permanent hardness (CaSO4) by washing soda: CaSO4 + Na2CO3 -> CaCO3 + Na2SO4. Town water treatment: screening, sedimentation, coagulation with alum, filtration, chlorination.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis while iron is extracted by reduction with carbon. [3 marks]
(b) In the extraction of iron in the blast furnace:
(i) name the three raw materials charged at the top; [3 marks]
(ii) write equations for the formation of the reducing agent and the reduction of haematite; [4 marks]
(iii) write equations to show how slag is formed and state one use of slag; [3 marks]
(iv) calculate the maximum mass of iron obtainable from 1.0 tonne (1000 kg) of pure iron(III) oxide. [3 marks]
(c) In the electrolytic extraction of aluminium:
(i) why is the alumina dissolved in molten cryolite? [2 marks]
(ii) write the equations for the reactions at the cathode and the anode; [4 marks]
(iii) why must the carbon anodes be replaced periodically? [2 marks]
(d) Give one use of aluminium related to a named property. [1 mark]
[Fe = 56, O = 16]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Aluminium is high in the reactivity series (1); its oxide is very stable and cannot be reduced by carbon at economical temperatures (1); iron is lower in the series so its oxide is reduced by carbon/CO (1)
3 marks: (b)(i) Iron ore (haematite), coke and limestone (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(ii) C + O2 -> CO2; CO2 + C -> 2CO (formation of carbon(II) oxide)
2 marks: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2
2 marks: (b)(iii) CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 (slag)
1 mark: Use: road construction / making cement / fertiliser
1 mark: (b)(iv) Moles Fe2O3 = 1 000 000 g/160 = 6250 mol
1 mark: Moles Fe = 2 x 6250 = 12 500 mol
1 mark: Mass Fe = 12 500 x 56 = 700 kg (0.70 tonne)
2 marks: (c)(i) Cryolite lowers the melting point of alumina (from about 2050 to about 950 degrees C), saving energy, and improves conductivity
2 marks: (c)(ii) Cathode: Al^3+ + 3e^- -> Al
2 marks: Anode: 2O^2- -> O2 + 4e^-
2 marks: (c)(iii) Oxygen liberated at the anode reacts with the hot carbon, burning it away to CO2
1 mark: (d) Any one: overhead cables (good conductor, light); cooking pots (good heat conductor, does not corrode); aircraft bodies (light, strong alloys); window frames (resists corrosion)
questions.explanation: Blast furnace: coke, limestone and haematite; CO reduces Fe2O3; CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 slag. 1000 kg Fe2O3 gives 700 kg of iron. Aluminium: alumina in molten cryolite is electrolysed; Al deposits at the cathode and the carbon anodes burn away in the oxygen produced.

questions.stem:
A is a solution of hydrochloric acid containing 3.65 g of HCl per dm^3. B is a solution made by dissolving 6.00 g of impure anhydrous sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3, in distilled water and making it up to 1.00 dm^3. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using methyl orange as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 24.80, initial 0.00; 1st: final 24.70, initial 0.50; 2nd: final 25.50, initial 1.20; 3rd: final 25.05, initial 0.80.
(a)(i) Tabulate the readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the average volume of A used from the three accurate titres. [2 marks]
(iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark]
(iv) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. [2 marks]
(b) From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) concentration of A in mol dm^-3; [2 marks]
(ii) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [3 marks]
(iii) concentration of pure Na2CO3 in B in g dm^-3; [2 marks]
(iv) percentage purity of the sodium trioxocarbonate(IV). [2 marks]
(c)(i) Why is phenolphthalein not suitable for this titration? [2 marks]
(ii) Why should the conical flask not be rinsed with B before use? [2 marks]
[H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Titres (cm^3): rough 24.80; accurate 24.20, 24.30, 24.25 (composite table of final, initial and volume rows, to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (24.20 + 24.30 + 24.25)/3 = 24.25 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Yellow to orange (pink/red if overshot)
2 marks: (a)(iv) Na2CO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) (formulae 1, balance 1)
2 marks: (b)(i) Molar mass HCl = 36.5 g mol^-1; concentration = 3.65/36.5 = 0.100 mol dm^-3
1 mark: (b)(ii) Moles of A in titre = 0.100 x 24.25/1000 = 2.425 x 10^-3 mol
1 mark: Mole ratio A : B = 2 : 1, so moles of B = 1.212 x 10^-3 mol
1 mark: Concentration of B = 1.212 x 10^-3 x 1000/25.0 = 0.0485 mol dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iii) Molar mass Na2CO3 = 106 g mol^-1; 0.0485 x 106 = 5.14 g dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iv) Percentage purity = 5.14/6.00 x 100 = 85.7% (accept 85-87%)
2 marks: (c)(i) Phenolphthalein changes colour at about pH 8-10, at the first (hydrogentrioxocarbonate) stage; the complete reaction with a strong acid ends at an acidic pH which methyl orange detects
2 marks: (c)(ii) Rinsing would leave extra B in the flask, increasing the amount of B beyond 25.0 cm^3 and giving a larger titre
questions.explanation: Accurate titres 24.20, 24.30, 24.25; mean 24.25 cm^3. A = 0.100 mol dm^-3; moles HCl = 2.425 x 10^-3; Na2CO3 = half = 1.212 x 10^-3 mol in 25.0 cm^3, so B = 0.0485 mol dm^-3 = 5.14 g dm^-3; purity = 85.7%.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:
A is 0.0200 mol dm^-3 potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII) solution. questions.stem:

questions.stem:
C is a mixture of two salts. Carry out the following tests (alternative to practical: the observations are given) and record inferences.
(a) C was shaken with distilled water and filtered. The residue was kept. Observation: part of C dissolved; a white residue remained; the filtrate was colourless. [2 marks]
(b)(i) A portion of the filtrate was warmed with sodium hydroxide solution. Observation: a colourless gas with a pungent smell was given off; it turned damp red litmus paper blue and formed dense white fumes with a glass rod dipped in concentrated HCl. [3 marks]
(ii) To another portion of the filtrate, dilute HNO3 was added followed by silver trioxonitrate(V) solution, and then excess aqueous ammonia. Observation: a white precipitate formed which dissolved in excess aqueous ammonia. [3 marks]
(c)(i) The residue was treated with dilute HNO3. Observation: effervescence; a colourless, odourless gas turned lime water milky. The residue dissolved to give a colourless solution. [3 marks]
(ii) Sodium hydroxide solution was added to the solution from (c)(i) dropwise and then in excess. Observation: a white gelatinous precipitate formed which dissolved in excess. [2 marks]
(iii) Aqueous ammonia was added to another portion, dropwise and then in excess. Observation: a white gelatinous precipitate formed which dissolved in excess. [2 marks]
(d) Name the two salts in C. [2 marks]
(e) Write ionic equations for (i) the reaction in (b)(ii); (ii) the formation of the precipitate in (c)(ii). [3 marks]

2 marks: NH4^+ present in the filtrate
1 mark: (b)(ii) Precipitate is AgCl

1 mark: (c)(i) Gas is CO2
2 marks: CO3^2- present in the residue

2 marks: (c)(iii) Zn^2+ confirmed (Zn(OH)2 dissolves in excess NH3 forming a complex; Al(OH)3 and Pb(OH)2 do not)

1 mark: Zinc trioxocarbonate(IV) (ZnCO3)

questions.stem:
D is a white crystalline salt. The following tests were carried out on D (observations given). State the inference from each test.
(a) D was heated strongly in a dry test tube. Observation: the crystals crackled (decrepitated); a brown gas was evolved and a glowing splint held at the mouth of the tube was rekindled; a residue which was reddish-brown when hot and yellow when cold remained. [4 marks]
(b) D was dissolved in distilled water. Observation: a colourless solution formed. [1 mark]
(c)(i) Sodium hydroxide solution was added to a portion of the solution dropwise, then in excess. Observation: white precipitate, soluble in excess. [2 marks]
(ii) Aqueous ammonia was added to another portion dropwise, then in excess. Observation: white precipitate, insoluble in excess. [2 marks]
(iii) Potassium iodide solution was added to a third portion. Observation: a bright yellow precipitate formed. [2 marks]
(d) To a portion of the solution, freshly prepared iron(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution was added, then concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid was poured carefully down the side of the tube. Observation: a brown ring formed at the junction of the two layers. [2 marks]
(e) Identify D. [2 marks]
(f) Write a balanced equation for the decomposition of D on heating. [3 marks]
(g) Name the brown gas and the gas that rekindled the splint. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) NO2 and O2 evolved: a trioxonitrate(V) of a heavy metal (not Na/K)
2 marks: Residue reddish-brown hot, yellow cold: PbO, so Pb^2+ suspected

2 marks: (c)(iii) PbI2 formed: Pb^2+ confirmed

questions.stem:

questions.markingGuide:

questions.stem:

(d) G was warmed with acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) solution. Observation: the orange solution turned green and a vinegar-like smell was detected. [3 marks]
(e) F and G were warmed with a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 and the mixture was poured into cold water. Observation: a pleasant fruity smell. [3 marks]
(f) G was shaken with bromine water. Observation: the orange colour persisted. [1 mark]
(g) Given that F and G each contain two carbon atoms, identify F and G. [2 marks]
(h) Write equations for the reactions in (a) and (e). [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Gas is CO2
2 marks: F is an acid: contains the -COOH (alkanoic acid) group
1 mark: (b) G is not an acid (no -COOH)
1 mark: (c) Gas is hydrogen
2 marks: G contains an -OH group (alkanol)
1 mark: (d) G is a reducing agent (Cr2O7^2- reduced to Cr^3+)
2 marks: G is a primary alkanol, oxidised to an alkanoic acid (ethanoic acid)
1 mark: (e) An ester is formed
2 marks: Esterification confirms F is an alkanoic acid and G an alkanol
1 mark: (f) G is saturated (no C=C)
1 mark: (g) F: ethanoic acid (CH3COOH)
1 mark: G: ethanol (C2H5OH)
2 marks: (h) CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
2 marks: CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O
questions.explanation: F liberates CO2 from NaHCO3 (alkanoic acid); G liberates H2 with sodium, is oxidised by dichromate to a vinegar-smelling acid and is saturated (primary alkanol). Together they form a fruity ester. F = ethanoic acid, G = ethanol.

questions.stem:
In an experiment to determine the solubility of a salt X at 30 degrees C, a saturated solution of X at that temperature was prepared and some of the clear solution was poured into a weighed evaporating dish. The results were: mass of empty dish = 28.40 g; mass of dish + saturated solution = 58.40 g; mass of dish + dry salt (after evaporation to constant mass) = 35.60 g.
(a) Calculate (i) the mass of the dry salt; (ii) the mass of water in the solution. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the solubility of X in g per 100 g of water at 30 degrees C. [2 marks]
(c) If the molar mass of X is 74.5 g mol^-1, calculate its solubility in mol per kg of water. [2 marks]
(d) Why was the dish heated to constant mass? [2 marks]
(e) State one precaution taken to ensure that the solution used was saturated at 30 degrees C. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) 35.60 - 28.40 = 7.20 g
1 mark: (ii) 58.40 - 35.60 = 22.80 g
2 marks: (b) 7.20/22.80 x 100 = 31.6 g per 100 g of water
2 marks: (c) 31.6 g per 100 g = 316 g per kg; 316/74.5 = 4.24 mol kg^-1
2 marks: (d) To make sure that all the water had been driven off (the salt was completely dry)
2 marks: (e) Any one: excess solid remained undissolved at 30 degrees C; the temperature was kept at 30 degrees C while sampling; the solution was filtered/decanted to avoid undissolved solid
questions.explanation: Salt = 7.20 g, water = 22.80 g; solubility = 31.6 g per 100 g water = 4.24 mol kg^-1 for a molar mass of 74.5 g mol^-1.

questions.stem:
Equal lengths (2 cm) of magnesium ribbon were dropped into 50 cm^3 portions of hydrochloric acid of different concentrations at the same temperature, and the time taken for the ribbon to disappear was recorded: concentration/mol dm^-3: 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00; time/s: 96, 48, 32, 24.
(a) Calculate 1/t for each experiment (in s^-1, to 4 decimal places). [2 marks]
(b) What is the relationship between the concentration of the acid and the rate of reaction? Use your values to support your answer. [3 marks]
(c) Predict the time for the ribbon to disappear in 0.75 mol dm^-3 acid. [2 marks]
(d) Name the gas evolved and give a test for it. [2 marks]
(e) Name one variable that was kept constant. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) 1/t: 0.0104, 0.0208, 0.0312, 0.0417 s^-1
1 mark: (b) Rate (1/t) is directly proportional to concentration
2 marks: Doubling concentration from 0.50 to 1.00 doubles 1/t (0.0104 to 0.0208); concentration x time is constant (48)
2 marks: (c) t = 48/0.75 = 64 s
2 marks: (d) Hydrogen; burns with a 'pop' sound when a lighted splint is applied
1 mark: (e) Any one: temperature; volume of acid; length/mass of magnesium ribbon
questions.explanation: 1/t values 0.0104, 0.0208, 0.0312, 0.0417 s^-1 rise in proportion to concentration (c x t = 48); in 0.75 mol dm^-3 acid t = 64 s.

questions.stem:
50.0 cm^3 of 1.00 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide at 28.5 degrees C was quickly added to 50.0 cm^3 of 1.00 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid at 28.7 degrees C in a plastic cup. The highest temperature reached by the stirred mixture was 35.3 degrees C.
(a) Calculate the average initial temperature and the temperature rise. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the heat evolved, assuming the solution has a density of 1.00 g cm^-3 and a specific heat capacity of 4.2 J g^-1 K^-1. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the amount of water formed and hence the enthalpy of neutralisation. [3 marks]
(d) Why is a plastic (polystyrene) cup used rather than a glass beaker? [1 mark]
(e) Why would the value obtained with ethanoic acid be less exothermic? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Average initial temperature = (28.5 + 28.7)/2 = 28.6 degrees C
1 mark: Rise = 35.3 - 28.6 = 6.7 K
2 marks: (b) Heat = 100 x 4.2 x 6.7 = 2814 J
1 mark: (c) n(H2O) = n(HCl) = 1.00 x 50.0/1000 = 0.0500 mol
2 marks: Delta H = -2814/0.0500 = -56280 J mol^-1 = -56.3 kJ mol^-1
1 mark: (d) Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat (good insulator) and has a low heat capacity, so less heat is lost
2 marks: (e) Ethanoic acid is weak/partially ionised; some of the heat released is used to complete its ionisation (an endothermic process)
questions.explanation: Average initial temperature 28.6 degrees C, rise 6.7 K; heat = 100 x 4.2 x 6.7 = 2814 J for 0.0500 mol water; Delta H(neutralisation) = -56.3 kJ mol^-1.

questions.stem:
A student heated a sample of blue hydrated copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI), CuSO4.xH2O, in a crucible until it turned white and the mass became constant. The results were: mass of crucible = 20.25 g; mass of crucible + hydrated salt = 25.24 g; mass of crucible + anhydrous salt = 23.44 g.
(a) Calculate the mass of (i) hydrated salt; (ii) anhydrous salt; (iii) water lost. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the amounts in moles of anhydrous CuSO4 and of water, and hence find x. [4 marks]
(c) State what would be observed if a few drops of water were added to the cooled white residue. [1 mark]
(d) Why was the crucible allowed to cool in a desiccator before weighing? [2 marks]
[CuSO4 = 159.5 g mol^-1; H2O = 18 g mol^-1]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) 25.24 - 20.25 = 4.99 g
1 mark: (ii) 23.44 - 20.25 = 3.19 g
1 mark: (iii) 4.99 - 3.19 = 1.80 g
1 mark: (b) n(CuSO4) = 3.19/159.5 = 0.0200 mol
1 mark: n(H2O) = 1.80/18 = 0.1000 mol
2 marks: x = 0.1000/0.0200 = 5.00, so x = 5 (CuSO4.5H2O)
1 mark: (c) The white solid turns blue and becomes warm
2 marks: (d) To prevent the anhydrous salt from absorbing moisture from the air while cooling (and to weigh it at room temperature)
questions.explanation: Hydrated salt 4.99 g, anhydrous 3.19 g, water 1.80 g; n(CuSO4) = 0.0200, n(H2O) = 0.1000, ratio 5.00, so x = 5.
